section: Some basic principles of biosignals propagation:
text:
Some basic principles of biosignals propagation:

```mermaid {theme:‘dark’, scale:0.9} flowchart LR
A(Biosignal propagation) 
B(Volume Conduction)
C(Impedance)
D(Spatial degradation)
E(Summation)
F(Orientation)

A --> E

---
title: volume conduction
level: 3
---

## Volume conduction

- Electrical fields spread in space instantly 
(electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light)
- Propagation medium: extracellular fluid
- Volume conduction is **good**: it allows to detect the phenomenon at a distance
- Volume conduction is **bad**: multiple sources get mixed

---
title: impedance
level: 3

---
## Impedance

- Resistance to propagation of the electrical field
- Mainly due to the outer layer of the skin
- It can be decreased through (mild) skin abrasion


---
title: spatial degradation
level: 3
---

## Spatial degradation

- The electrical field is stronger near its source
- Its magnitude diminishes gradually the farther from the source

---
title: summation
level: 3
---

## Summation

- Most electro-chemical events are very small and involve few cells
- Because of their small magnitude and of spatial degradation, _in principle_ we cannot detect them from the skin
- However... small electro-chemical potentials can _summate_ into a larger potential when the individual potentials occur:
    - at the same time
    - in the same area
    - with roughly the same orientation (more on this in the next slide)

---
layout: two-cols
title: orientation
level: 3
---

## Orientation

- Each electrical event has a geometry: a dipole
- Just like vectors, multiple dipoles have a _resultant_
- Dipoles in the same orientation _summate_ and their resultant is larger than the individual dipoles
- Dipoles in the opposite orientation _cancel out_ and their resultant is smaller than the individual dipoles (or even null)
- Not all resulting dipoles are big enough to be detectable from the skin

::right::

<img src="/images/neuronDipole.jpg" style="height:100%; margin:auto" >

title: acquisition

# Biosignals: 
## acquisition

title: the recording chain
level: 2

## Overarching objective:
- Measure the electrical field associated with the biological event (the <span v-mark.circle.orange="1">**signal**</span>)
- While discarding as much as possible of other biological (or not biological) events (the <span v-mark.circle.orange="1">**noise**</span>)
- makimize signal to noise ratio: 
  $SNR = \frac{S}{N}$

## The recording chain:

title: More to come
text:
Sensors: Electrodes
Conductive material
Used in pairs to measure a difference in voltage Note: One electrode alone cannot measure anything
At the interface between electrode and skin, electro-chemical reactions occur consisting of exchange of ions.
The exchange of ion generates an unwanted voltage, called offset potential or bias potential
Desirable property of electrodes: stability against offset potential
Factors affecting electrode stability: - temperature - electrolyte composition (between the electrode and the skin) - metal type (the electrode)
Lykken (1959)1 experimented with different metals.
Left pairs of electrode pairs of various metals in a saline solution (electrolyte) for 1 hour.
Among several metals such as platinum, zinc, silver, Ag/AgCl2 showed the lowest offset potential. To this day, mosty electrodes are made of this metal.
Desirable property of skin-electrode interface low impedance, so the signal passes through with little resistance. skin –> electrolytic gel –> electrode
Skin preparation to lower impedance: - mild abrasion with sandpaper or abrasive paste (scrub) to remove dead cells - alcohol to clean residuals - More abrasion –> lower impedance - Larger signals (e.g., ECG) can be ok even with less abrasion
Lykken, D. T. (1959). Properties of electrode used in electrodermal measurement. Journal of Comparative and Physiological Psychology, 52(5), 629.Ag/AgCl = “chlorided silver” or “silver / silver chloride” meaning silver coated with silver chloride

title: More to come
text:
Sensors: Transducers
While biological events have electrical nature, certain electrical fields are difficult to detect. Non-electrical consequences of these events are easier to detect
Transducers convert (transduce) non-electrical signals to electrical signals (for the next steps of the recording chain)
Examples:
::left::

title: Learning resources
text:
changes in blood volume
Photo-conductive transducer: - infra-red (IR) light is sent from a light emitter - IR-light passes through certain biological tissues (e.g., skin) but it is reflected back by other tissues (e.g., blood) - By measuring the difference between IR-light emitted and received back, we can infer blood volume - commonly placed on finger or earlobe

title: Learning resources
text:
changes in pupil diameter
Photo-sensitive transducer:

infra-red (IR) light is sent from a light emitter
IR-light is reflected differently by pupil and iris
By measuring the areas with more and less IR-light reflection, we can infer the size of the diameter
pupillometry

title: More to come
text:
Coupler

Transmits the electrical signal from the sensor to the amplifier.
Optionally: - it powers the transducer - basic computations (e.g., filtering)
Filtering is a complex mechanism… Let’s first see waveforms of different frequencies

basic filter types

title: Learning resources
text:
Low-pass
Filters out fast (high) frequencies and retains slow (low) frequencies

title: Learning resources
text:
High-pass
Filters out slow (low) frequencies and retains fast (high) frequencies
Both filters require: - cut-off frequency value - other parameters having to do with how sharp the transition is from filtered frequencies to non-filtered frequencies

title: Learning resources
text:
Band-pass
a combination of high-pass and low-pass filters to allow frequencies between two cut-off values, which describe a frequency band. Frequencies outside of this band are filtered out
Depending on the sharpness parameter, frequencies near the transition are partly retained
In theory, a filter with a sharp transition is better. In practice, too sharp will create distortions

title: Learning resources
text:
Notch
Filters out only one frequency (and those immediately near t) Used to minimize the electrical interference from mains electricity (alternative current). In the UK, it is 50 Hz

title: More to come
text:
Amplifier

Multiplies the filtered signal
The multiplication factor is called gain
Traditionally, so the magnitude of the signal reaches approximately 1 V.
For example, a signal with magnitude 1 mV will be multiplied by 1000 to reach 1 V. In this example, the gain is 1000.
Note: Important to amplify the noise but not the signal. That’s why filtering happens before amplifying (with some exceptions)

title: More to come
text:
Visualization and storage
Analog signal

continuous.
Imagine an uninterrupted line on a polygraph.

Digital signal

discrete.
Ir has small temporal gaps between each value. Imagine taking a a sample (value) every so often and storing each sample. If the samples are taken very often, the gaps between samples will be small.

Sampling rate: how many samples are taken in a unit of time

title: Learning resources
text:
Analog-to-digital conversion
Computers can only store digital signals. But the acquired electrical signals are analog
The computer samples the analog signal at a certain rate to store a digital copy.
The digital copy of the analog signal is an approximation of the original analog signal
The higher the sampling rate, the better the digital copy. However, higher sampling rate needs more digital storage/memory.
The lower the sampling rate the less digital storage/memory is required. However, too low sampling rate leads to distortion.
Analogy for the analog-to-digital conversion: Imagine you want to convert a 1-min video into a number of screenshots that can decently represent what’s in the video. How often do you take a screenshot? It depends on what’s in the video…
Distortion due to using a too-small sampling rate is called aliasing
To avoid aliasing, the sampling rate should be at least 2-5 times larger than the larger frequency contained in the signal.

text: processing

title: Learning resources
text:
Signal reduction
Term indicating the signal processing happening before statistics are run. For example:

Reduce the complex ECG waveform into a simpler series of heart rate (HR) values
Reduce the complex EOG waveform into a simpler number of eye blinks within a minute

Signal reduction can happen:

Online (during the acquisition stage, in real time)
Offline (after the acquisition stage)

title: Learning resources
text:
signal processing
The temporal dynamics of biological activity can be classified in: - tonic - phasic

title: Learning resources
text:
tonic activity

Background level over a relatively long period of time
Useful for studying the signal “on average”
Generally recorded at rest, but it could be recorded during a relatively long activity
Sometimes interesting as a baseline for phasic acitivyt (next slide); sometimes interesting by itself (e.g., essential hypertension)

title: Learning resources
text:
phasic activity

Transient activity over a relatively short period of time
Useful for studying the short-lived fluctuations on top of tonic activity
Generally specific to reaction to certain events (e.g., a stimulus is presented that needs processing, an action is performed)
It can be a change in amplitude of the signal, frequency of the signal, or other (more complex) parameters not discussed in this module

title: Learning resources
text:
Change scores
General idea: describe transient changes (phasic activity) from baseline (tonic activity)
Where: A = activity; B = baseline
Notable types of change scores:

Subtraction: \(A - B\)
Percentage change: \(\frac{A-B}{B} \times 100\)
Decibel change: \(10 \log_{10}\frac{A}{B}\)

title: Learning resources
text:
Time domain
Features that develop over time. For example:

Durations (e.g., eye blink duration)
Rate (e.g., number of ECG R-waves in 1 minute)
Amplitude (e.g., max blood pressure)

title: Learning resources
text:
frequency domain (aka: spectral)
Features linked to trends. For example: - the magnitude of oscillations at certain frequencies - the positioning of oscillations at certain frequencies

title: Learning resources
text:
Coherence
Extent to which two signals are related:

Within the same biological domain (e.g., connectivity between brain areas)
Across biological domains (e.g., coupling between breathing rate and heart rate)

a combination of high-pass and low-pass filters to allow frequencies between two cut-off values, which describe a frequency band. Frequecies outside of this band are filtered out

Analog-to-digital conversion
Computers can only store digital signals. But the acquired electrical signals are analog
The computer samples the analog signal at a certain rate to store a digital copy.
The digital copy of the analog signal is an approximation of the original analog signal
The higher the sampling rate, the better the digital copy. However, higher sampling rate needs more digital storage/memory.
The lower the sampling rate the less digital storage/memory is required. However, too low sampling rate leads to distortion.
Analogy for the analog-to-digital conversion: Imagine you want to convert a 1-min video into a number of screenshots that can decently represent what’s in the video. How often do you take a screenshot? It depends on what’s in the video…

title: Learning resources
text:
EOG calibration
::left::
The native units of the EOG are Volts, but eye movements are better described as visual angles.
This is because eye movements are angular (rotation of the eyeball).
Calibration allows to compute how many Volts correspond to 1 degree of visual angle.
Then we can convert EOG from Volts to degrees.
::right::

title: Learning resources
section: Physiological source of the EOG blink
text:
Physiological source of the EOG blink

Not as well understood as the source of eye movements (corneoretinal potential)

Initially thought to be due to upward rotation of the eyeball (rapid dipole rotation)
More recently thought to be due to eyelid bridging the corneoretinal positivity with the forehead (changes in electrical conductivity)

title: Learning resources
text:
EOG Blink wave characteristics



Typical duration: 200-400 ms
Biphasic pattern

Initial positive deflection
Followed by negative component

Amplitude typically larger than saccades
More prominent in vertical than horizontal channels

title: Learning resources
text:
EOG Limitations

While EOG is a useful technique, it has some limitations:


Signal noise: EOG signals can be affected by electrical noise from other sources, such as muscle activity and external electronic devices.
Artifact contamination: Blinks and other involuntary eye movements can introduce artifacts into the EOG signal, complicating data analysis.
head movement confounders: EOG saccadic signals reflect movements of the eyeballs relative to the head. By looking at the EOG only or without behavioural constrains, it is difficult to know whether the eyes, the head, or both have moved.
Limited spatial resolution: EOG provides less precise information about the exact point of gaze compared to other eye-tracking methods, such as video-based eye trackers.
Calibration drift: The corneoretinal potential can change over time, requiring frequent recalibration.

title: Learning resources
text:
Future Directions
Research and development in EOG technology are ongoing, with several promising directions:


Improved signal processing: Developing advanced algorithms to reduce noise and artifacts in EOG signals. A promising technique is median filtering1.
Integration with other modalities: Combining EOG with other physiological measurements, such as EEG and EMG, for a more comprehensive understanding of human behavior.2
Wearable EOG devices: Creating portable and user-friendly EOG systems for real-world applications, such as sports training and assistive technology.

Common artifacts

Muscular: high-frequency, localized to scalp/neck/face regions
Blinking: large-amplitude deflections in frontal channels
Eye movements: slower deflections proportional to gaze movement
Electrode-related: sudden baseline shifts or noise spikes

Frequency bands and alpha

Alpha (8-12 Hz): Often associated with relaxation and cortical inhibition
Can be volitionally modulated through relaxation or cognitive engagement
Regional specificity aids in understanding task-related brain activity

Fourier transform: Converts time-domain signal to frequency domain for spectral analysis
ERP (Event-Related Potential): Averaged EEG activity time-locked to a specific event
P300: Late positive component (300+ ms post-stimulus) associated with attention and cognitive processing

title: Practical 1 · Your first data point
text:
Welcome
This module is about the journey a signal makes from your senses to your muscles, and everything the brain does along the way. Before any lecture, we are going to time that journey. In an hour you will know the module; right now you only need a phone or laptop and a neighbour. Turn to that neighbour now: name, course, sport you care about. You are a pair for the next 50 minutes.

title: Practical 1 · Your first data point
text:
Aim
Measure your own reaction time and build the class’s first dataset.

title: Practical 1 · Your first data point
text:
Predict
Before measuring anything, each of you answers question 1 in the form. Guess honestly, no searching.

title: Practical 1 · Your first data point
text:
Steps
One of you does the task first while the other reads these steps and writes the numbers down, then swap.

Open humanbenchmark.com/tests/reactiontime on your phone or laptop.
Read the instructions on screen: when the red screen turns green, tap or click as fast as you can.
Do 5 trials. Do not restart if a trial goes badly; that is part of the measurement.
After the fifth trial the site shows your average. Your partner writes it down.
Look back at the five individual times and write down the fastest one.
Note what you used: phone, laptop or tablet.
Swap roles and repeat.
Round 2. Do the whole test again, same hand, another 5 trials. Write down the new average. Swap and repeat.
Before you submit, look at your two averages side by side. Same? Different? Hold that thought.

title: Practical 1 · Your first data point
text:
Submit
Open the form at link 1 again. This time answer Results:
Enter your round 1 average and fastest, your round 2 average, and your device. That is your first data point in this module.

title: Practical 1 · Your first data point
text:
What to notice
Discuss these with your partner first. Then we look at the anonymised class data on the screen together.

How much did the room disagree with itself? What is the gap between the fastest and slowest average in the class?
Was the class’s prediction close to what it measured? In which direction was it wrong?
Did phones and laptops give the same numbers? If not, who is right: the people, or the devices?
You measured yourself twice. Did you get the same answer? If your two averages differ by 20 ms, is one of them the “real” you?
A laboratory measurement of the same thing, with a finger resting on a key, comes out around 200–250 ms. Where does our class sit, and what might explain any difference?

title: Practical 1 · Your first data point
text:
If you have time

Your fastest trial is quicker than your average. Which of the two is the better description of you? Why might a coach prefer one and a scientist the other?
Compare your average with your partner’s. Is one of you faster, or is the difference small enough that a second set of five trials could flip it? What would convince you the difference is real? (Keep your answer; we return to it in Week 3.)



If the test did not work on your device

Use these numbers so you can still take part in the discussion: round 1 average 268 ms, fastest 221 ms; round 2 average 259 ms; phone.

The familiar route


H0   ·   statistic   ·   null distribution   ·   p = tail area


     36 differences t = … t 


Draw live (D1): dots in the left box (the paired differences, some +, some −) → arrow → one number t → the bell curve over the pre-placed axis → shade the right tail → write p.

The bell curve was never computed from our data



one feature: channel Fz at ~400 ms
t-distribution, df = 35
a theoretical prediction of how t behaves when nothing is going on
valid if the assumptions hold

title: Learning resources
section: A p-value is a tail area under a null distribution
text:
A p-value is a tail area under a null distribution

Today we keep that definition and change only where the distribution comes from:

parametric — predicted from theory
empirical — built from the data


The resampling family: permutation, bootstrap, jackknife (Ernst, 2004).

title: Learning resources
section: Exchangeability: which rearrangements are equally plausible under H0?
text:
Exchangeability: which rearrangements are equally plausible under H0?


within-subject: swapping the two conditions inside one person is invisible to H0 → the difference score flips sign
between-subject: shuffling the group labels across people


Maris & Oostenveld (2007), §4.2.3 and §5.

One draw from the world where H0 is true






Left: the 36 Fz difference scores as they are. Right: the same dots after one random sign-flip. This is one draw from the world where H0 is true and OUR data are what they are.

histogram of t from 10k sign-flips
the figure shows |t|: a two-sided test becomes one-sided in |t|
236 rearrangements exist; we sample 10k (Monte Carlo)
p = proportion at or beyond the observed

Where they agree, nothing was lost; where they disagree, trust the one built from the data.

What was gained, and what was not

Gained:

no normality assumption
any statistic you like
a p-value conditional on your own sample (Maris & Oostenveld, 2007, §4.3.2)

Not gained:

independence between participants is still assumed

Run the test at every feature, report what lights up






The observed t-map across the tested 200–600 ms window, 6,560 features, contours where uncorrected p < .05. This is what you get if you run Part 2 at every feature and report what lights up.

title: Learning resources
section: A world where nothing is going on
text:
A world where nothing is going on






One null rearrangement’s t-map with its own p < .05 points. Count the beans. Family-wise error rate: the probability of at least one false positive across the family.

title: Learning resources
section: Bonferroni corrects for tests that were never run
text:
Bonferroni corrects for tests that were never run


Bonferroni: 0.05 / 6560
neighbouring features are strongly correlated
the correction assumes independent tests — for EEG they were never run
the exact FWER cannot even be computed without knowing that dependence


Maris & Oostenveld (2007), footnote 1; Groppe, Urbach, & Kutas (2011).

title: Learning resources
section: We need a correction that knows how correlated our features are
text:
We need a correction that knows how correlated our features are


We already have one.

title: Learning resources
text:
Keep the max |t|


              d (observed) grid of t d̂₁ d̂₂ d̂₃ … × 10k S(·) count 


(Maris & Oostenveld, 2007, §4.4.1; Blair & Karniski, 1993; Nichols & Holmes, 2002)


The multiple comparisons problem disappears because thousands of tests are replaced by ONE statistic for the whole grid. maxT is the simplest such statistic. Write “keep max |t|” in the empty dashed box.

text:
Every observed t against the distribution of maxima






Diagonale’s diagnostic figure, feature level: histogram of the maximum |t| per rearrangement, threshold, observed values. If the largest is not exceptional, none is. Because the maxima come from our own correlated data, the correction adapts to that correlation; the parametric route cannot offer this.

Family-wise control came free with the empirical null


One extra line in a loop we already had.

title: Learning resources
section: Effects in EEG are extended in time and space
text:
Effects in EEG are extended in time and space


ask about neighbourhoods, not points
a test statistic can encode that prior knowledge
the nonparametric framework lets us use any statistic


Maris & Oostenveld (2007), §4.4.2; cluster mass from Bullmore et al. (1999).

Step 1: the map you were told to distrust






The uncorrected map from Part 3 is step 1 here, but it is only used to draw boundaries, never to make claims. The forming threshold affects sensitivity, not validity (Maris & Oostenveld, 2007, §3.1.1).

title: Learning resources

text:
Who is a neighbour of whom















Neighbour in time = adjacent samples. Neighbour in space = electrodes within an angular distance — 0.63 rad for this 32-channel montage. The choice is yours and must be reported.

Clusters: connected neighbourhoods above threshold






Cluster statistic: mass = sum of t inside the cluster. Size and max are alternatives.

Observed clusters against the distribution of maximum masses






Diagonale’s diagnostic figure, cluster level: histogram of the maximum cluster mass per rearrangement, threshold, observed clusters. Read it as before: if the biggest observed mass is not exceptional among the maxima, no cluster is.

title: Learning resources

text:
What the p is a p-value of


it belongs to the cluster’s existence
not to any point in it, not to its boundaries
extent and latency are descriptive
the forming threshold changes what is found: weak-and-broad vs strong-and-focal


Maris & Oostenveld (2007), §4.2.2 (weak control) and Conclusions; Sassenhagen & Draschkow (2019).

text:
The same numbers, laid out as a grid






Exactly the same data: each line becomes one row of the image, colour is the value the line was showing (θ power in dB, see the colorbar). 32 channels by 614 time points; the 200–600 ms window we will test holds 32 × 205 = 6,560 numbers per person. We want to know whether two conditions (high vs low workload) differ. The promise: by 11:30 you will be able to read a cluster result and say exactly what its p-value is a p-value OF.

text:
8 Images: inclusion and resizing
Basic form:
![alt text](path/or/url.png){width=50%}
Alt text is written to the html; keep it descriptive (accessibility and screen readers).

8.1 Size
{width=50%}                 % of the container (slide or column)
{width=400px}               absolute
{height=300px}              absolute; width follows aspect ratio
{width=50% height=200px}    both set = distortion unless ratio matches
{width=50% fig-align="center"}   left | center | right


8.2 The auto-stretch trap
A slide containing a single image (and little else) is auto-stretched by revealjs to fill the vertical space; width= is then ignored. Fixes, in order of preference:

# Title {.nostretch} on the slide heading, then width= is respected.
Put the image inside a column; stretching does not apply inside .columns.
Add more content to the slide (a caption or paragraph breaks the lone-image condition).

The reverse, forcing an image to fill remaining height:
![](img.png){.r-stretch}


8.3 Resize via the column
Usually the cleanest method: give the image width=100% and control size with the column width.
::::{.columns}
:::{.column width=35%}
![](img.png){width=100%}
:::
:::{.column width=65%}
text
:::
::::


8.4 Pinned placement
![](img.png){.absolute top=100 left=50 width=300}
![](img.png){.absolute bottom=0 right=0 width=200 height=150}
Units are px relative to the 1280 × 720 canvas. Stacking pinned images with .fragment works.


8.5 Raw HTML fallback
When Quarto attributes are not enough (e.g. max-height, borders, object-fit):
<img src="img.png" style="width:40%; max-height:500px; object-fit:contain; border:1px solid #4c566a;">
Raw <img> is not auto-stretched and does not get a caption.


8.6 Captions and lightbox
![Caption text](img.png){width=60% fig-cap="Caption text"}
![](img.png){width=60% .lightbox}
![](img.png){width=60% .lightbox group="brain"}   # click-to-enlarge, grouped gallery
A caption takes ~1 line of vertical space; on a full slide drop it or use title= for a hover tooltip instead ({title="Alan Baddeley"}).


8.7 Side-by-side images
Two options: two columns (each image width=100%), or a layout block:
::: {layout-ncol=2}
![](a.png)
![](b.png)
:::

::: {layout="[60,40]"}
![](a.png)
![](b.png)
:::


8.8 Image as slide background
# Title {background-image="img.png" background-size="contain" background-opacity=0.4}
background-size: cover (default, crops) | contain (fits, letterboxes). background-position="top left" also available.

text:
18 Gotchas

Blank line missing around a ::: fence → fence rendered as literal colons.
Lone image ignores width= → add .nostretch to the heading.
Iframe or image with height="100%" → collapses; use px.
Bullets appear one by one unexpectedly → incremental: true is global; use .nonincremental.
Content cut at the bottom → slide is 720 px and scrollable: false; add {.scrollable} or split.
Shortcode shows as raw text → extension not installed in this project.
**bold** inside a <div> not rendered → blank lines after <div> and before </div>.
Percent widths in columns not adding up → last column wraps under the first.
## heading behaving like # → expected; navigation-mode: linear.
Text too small on the projector → custom.css sets 0.95em; raise per slide with <div style="font-size:1.2em"> rather than editing the css.
PDF export loses QR code and PIN → they are wrapped in content-visible when-format="html", by design.
Images by URL disappear later → external hosts change; copy important images into an img/ folder.

title: Practical 2 · The nervous system, timed
text:
Aim
Time a signal as it passes through a whole row of nervous systems, and find out how much of a reaction is nerve conduction and how much is everything else. Links to today’s lecture: the “why are we not faster?” calculation and the five stages of a reaction.

title: Practical 2 · The nervous system, timed
text:
Set up your chain
Your row is a chain. Aim for 8 to 12 people; split or merge rows if needed. In each chain:

One person at the end is the starter. They give the first signal and do not react to anything.
One person is the timer. They stand where they can see both ends, with a stopwatch open on their phone.
Everyone else reacts. Count how many of you there are. That number is N.

Nobody touches anybody. The signal travels by sound or by sight.

title: Practical 2 · The nervous system, timed
text:
Predict
Answer question 1 in the form: how many milliseconds do you think each person will add to the chain? You have just seen a number in the lecture. Use it if you want to.

title: Practical 2 · The nervous system, timed
text:
Steps
Chains go one at a time, so the room stays quiet for whoever is running.
A. By sound

Everyone who reacts closes their eyes. Starter and timer keep theirs open.
The starter claps once, loudly. The timer starts the stopwatch on that clap.
Each person claps as soon as they hear the person before them clap.
The timer stops the stopwatch on the last clap and calls out the time.
Do this three times. Timer writes down all three (seconds, two decimals).

B. By sight

Eyes open. Everyone turns to watch the person before them. Complete silence.
The starter raises a hand. Each person raises a hand as soon as they see the previous hand go up.
The timer stops on the last hand. Three runs, all three written down.

title: Practical 2 · The nervous system, timed
text:
Submit
The timer submits for the chain: N and the six totals (questions 2 to 9). Everyone else has already submitted their prediction.
Open the form: LINK

title: Practical 2 · The nervous system, timed
text:
What to notice
Discuss in pairs first, then we look at the class data on the screen.

Divide one of your totals by N, then multiply by 1000. That is milliseconds per person. How does it compare with the 155 ms from the lecture?
Which was faster, sound or sight? Is the difference in the direction the lecture predicted?
Did run 3 come out faster than run 1? What changed between them: the nervous system, or something else?
The chain measures five stages of a reaction, N times over. Which stages does a clap add that a finger-on-a-key does not?

title: Practical 2 · The nervous system, timed
text:
If you have time

Work out how many milliseconds of your per-person time is nerve conduction, using the lecture’s estimate (about 40 ms). What fraction is left over, and what is it?
Your timer’s thumb reacted twice, once at the start and once at the end. Roughly how much error does that put into the total? And how much per person, after dividing by N?
Sprinters are disqualified if they leave the blocks less than 100 ms after the gun. Given what you measured today, why is 100 ms the line?



If your chain’s numbers went missing

Use this chain: N = 9. By sound: 2.91 s, 2.64 s, 2.48 s. By sight: 3.62 s, 3.40 s, 3.15 s.

title: Practical 1 · Your first data point
text:
TASK 2
Work with your partner to measure your reaction time. One of you does the task while the other reads these steps and writes the numbers down. Then swap roles.

Open LINK 2 on your phone or laptop (or use the QR code).



    

Read the instructions on screen: when the red screen turns green, tap or click as fast as you can.
Do 5 trials. Do not restart if a trial goes badly; that is part of the measurement.
After each trial the site shows that trial’s time before you click on. Your partner writes down every one of the five.
At the end the site shows your average. Your partner writes that down too, then circles the fastest of the five.
Note what you used: phone, laptop or tablet.
Swap roles and repeat.
Round 2. Do the whole test again, same hand, another 5 trials. This time only the new average is needed. Swap and repeat.
Before you submit, look at your two averages side by side. Same? Different? Hold that thought.

Open the form at link 1 again. This time answer Results:

title: Practical 1 · Your first data point
text:
What to notice
Discuss these with your partner first. Then we look at the anonymised class data on the screen together.

How much did the room disagree with itself? What is the gap between the fastest and slowest average in the class?
Was the class’s prediction close to what it measured? In which direction was it wrong?
Did phones and laptops give the same numbers? If not, who is right: the people, or the devices?
You measured yourself twice. Did you get the same answer? If your two averages differ by 20 ms, is one of them the “real” you?
A laboratory measurement of the same thing, with a finger resting on a key, comes out around 200–250 ms. Where does our class sit, and what might explain any difference?

title: Practical 1 · Your first data point
text:
If you have time

Your fastest trial is quicker than your average. Which of the two is the better description of you? Why might a coach prefer one and a scientist the other?
Compare your average with your partner’s. Is one of you faster, or is the difference small enough that a second set of five trials could flip it? What would convince you the difference is real? (Keep your answer; we return to it in Week 3.)



If the test did not work on your device

Use these numbers so you can still take part in the discussion: round 1 average 268 ms, fastest 221 ms; round 2 average 259 ms; phone.
